title: Honolulu, the draft and the 25th Infantry jazz band
summary: The band is drafted in Honolulu in 1917 and enlisted together into the 25th Infantry, moving to the Mexican border where soldiers love their jazz band and the Colonel lets them sell punch.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: What happened to him? Did he leave California?

I'm gonna tell you about him. And so, we...uh ...I'm working down here. We came down here in '17, and Wells was drafted, and he...they took him to war, so that time, we put Ernest Coycault--you know who he is--Ernest Johnson, the trumpet player with the Black and Tan. We hired him to work with us in Wells's place. Then we...I got a letter here someplace...they wanted us in Honolulu at the...at the...uh...that big hotel over there...can't think of it now. Anyway, after we stayed our time down here--I think it was a year or something like that--we decided to go to Honolulu, and when we got in Honolulu, two of us was drafted. I was drafted, and then

the Queen's Throne Room was where the draft office was, in the Queen's Palace. So I was drafted in the Queen's Palace in Honolulu, and there was another boy drafted, and Slocum and a couple of other boys enlisted so we'd all stay together, and we all went in, and Wells was...they had discharged Wells, and he came back with us to Honolulu. He came to Honolulu and rejoined us. But he enlisted again, and we all went right into the Army together as the band in the Twenty-fifth Infantry, and we never went to France because the Twenty-Fifth Infantry was stationed in Honolulu, and we never had to lose our jobs. They let us work on the roof garden there as long as they stayed there, which was about four or five weeks after we were drafted. They picked the Twenty-Fifth Infantry up and brought it to the States, and that was when the Mexicans was raising sand down there and they sent us to...uh...down in Mexico there to the border. I can't think of the town. Anyway, they sent us down there, and they passed a law on the...there in the camp...that they...you couldn't charge anything for dancing. They all soldiers, you know... three or four thousand soldiers...they wanted us to play, for the dances. They didn't like the soldier band because it was just Compta-oompta...you know...regular straight old beat on...and we had all that jazz and stuff, and they was crazy about it, so...so we all played in the band. They put us all in the band, and so the Colonel give us a break--he let us charge for the punch. So we charged a half a dollar a glass for the punch and give the dance free. So, every Saturday night, we made twenty-five or thirty dollars.

We was new, and they was crazy about the jazz band, so all the soldiers was bringing them Mexican girls. The white girls...uh, I mean the colored girls they could find around and everything, and their wives--a lot of them had wives--and we'd have a dance every Saturday night, and they...we...during the week, we'd play downtown in the picture show, and we...they had...you know, you had Reveille at eleven o'clock. We never did have to make it because we didn't get out of the theater until eleven, so we could stay out all night if we wanted. [Laughs] So the Colonel was so crazy about the jazz band. He asked for us when we were drafted in Honolulu, he asked for us, permission from the War Company...you know, the War...

...Department to let us go into the Twenty-Fifth Infantry 'cause he had the best football players, and he had the best baseball players. He had Billard Rogan and all them people in his Twenty-Fifth Infantry Band and he had the best runners. He had every best thing that the soldiers could do. He had it in his company but he never had a jazz band so he wanted a jazz band so they gave him permission so he brought us to Arizona, and we stayed down there on the border, and all this happened down there till the war was over.
